answers.answer:
Short answer: because SCOPe family membership is a statement about common ancestry of a repeat module, not about chain length. In a.298.1.1 the classifying unit is the ~33-35 residue TAL effector repeat (a two-helix alpha1-loop-alpha2 module) and the tandem right-handed superhelical solenoid it builds. Repeat copy number is a modular, copy-number-variable trait that changes length by an order of magnitude while leaving fold, superfamily, and family identity untouched.

Why length is uninformative here

1. Modularity. One TAL effector repeat recognizes one DNA base pair, so natural and engineered TALEs carry anywhere from a few to more than 30 repeats. Adding or deleting repeats changes the length of the DNA target, not the architecture. A 1-2 repeat construct and a 23.5-repeat effector present the same fold: the same helix packing, the same inter-repeat interface, the same superhelical handedness.

2. Extreme scaffold conservation. The TAL effector repeat is nearly invariant outside positions 12 and 13 (the repeat-variable diresidue, RVD). Because positions 1-11 and 14-33/35 are conserved, homology is trivially detectable between a short fragment and a long array, which is exactly the evidence SCOPe needs for a family-level (clear common ancestry, usually with sequence support) assignment rather than a mere superfamily or fold grouping.

3. SCOPe domain definition. All three identifiers end in the whole-chain suffix (the trailing underscore in d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, d4cj9a_), meaning SCOPe treats the entire chain as a single domain. For solenoids SCOPe does not split the array into per-repeat domains, so the domain length simply inherits the construct length deposited in the PDB. Much of the apparent length disparity is a construct and domain-definition artifact, not a structural distinction.

The three named entities (identities to verify in the PDB header before use)

- d3v6pa_: PDB 3V6P, the Xanthomonas TAL effector PthXo1 in complex with its double-stranded DNA target. This is the long member, a near-full-length central repeat region of roughly 23.5 repeats plus N-terminal cryptic repeats, on the order of 900+ modeled residues. DNA-bound state.
- d2kq5a_: an NMR entry, and the short member, a minimal construct covering only one or a few repeats, on the order of tens of residues. Because it is a solution structure of a truncated array, it has no bound DNA and its superhelical context is absent.
- d4cj9a_: a later crystal structure of a TAL effector-like repeat protein, intermediate in length. I am not confident whether this is a Ralstonia RipTAL/Brg11-type protein, a Burkholderia TALE-like (Bat/BurrH-type) protein, or an engineered TALE variant. Confirm the molecule name, organism, and repeat count from the PDB entry before treating it as either a natural TALE orthologue or a designed scaffold, because that distinction changes how its specificity data should be read.

The length ordering above should be confirmed from SEQRES and the SCOPe class file rather than taken from my recollection.

Hierarchy level and what each level does and does not license

- Class a: all-alpha proteins. Carries no functional meaning whatsoever.
- Fold a.298: the two-helix repeat solenoid geometry. At fold level this superficially resembles other alpha-solenoids such as ankyrin, HEAT, and armadillo repeats, but SCOPe keeps TAL effector repeats as a separate fold. Do not infer TALE-style major-groove base readout from any other alpha-solenoid fold, and do not infer a common ancestor from the shared solenoid shape.
- Superfamily a.298.1 and family a.298.1.1: common ancestry, supported by the conserved repeat consensus. Family membership here does license the inference of a shared repeat architecture and shared mode of assembly.

Unsafe transfers to avoid

- DNA specificity is not a family property. The RVD code (positions 12-13) differs repeat-by-repeat and protein-by-protein. You cannot transfer the target sequence of PthXo1 to either of the other two members. Specificity must come from the actual repeat sequence of the specific protein.
- Function is not guaranteed by membership. A one- or few-repeat NMR construct will not bind DNA with useful affinity on its own; cooperative wrapping requires many repeats plus the N-terminal cryptic repeats (including the -1 and 0 repeats that read the 5' thymine) and the C-terminal half repeat. Those elements, and the TALE activation domain and nuclear localization signals, lie outside the SCOPe domain entirely, so SCOPe membership says nothing about transcriptional activation or virulence.
- Template use. Do not use the short member as a homology-modeling or docking template for a long array. Repeat number, superhelical pitch, and DNA-bound versus apo conformation all differ; apo TALEs are measurably more extended and relaxed than the compressed, DNA-wrapped state, so a free short fragment propagates the wrong twist when tiled. Use a length-matched, DNA-bound template such as the PthXo1 or Hax3 complexes.
- Representative selection. ASTRAL subsets filtered at 40% or even 95% sequence identity will collapse these members because scaffold identity is high, and the surviving representative may be the shortest or an NMR entry. That is a poor structural representative for the family. Choose by repeat count, ligand state, and resolution rather than accepting the default identity-filtered pick.

Required external evidence

PDB entry headers plus SEQRES and resolution or NMR method for true construct lengths and repeat counts; SCOPe parseable files (dir.cla, dir.des, dir.hie) for the sid-to-sunid mapping and the exact hierarchy; ASTRAL for representative sets; repeat annotation such as Pfam PF03377 or a TALE repeat finder to count repeats and extract RVDs; and primary literature for the RVD-to-base code and for any reported binding data.

Release specificity

a.298 is a high-numbered fold that does not exist in the original SCOP 1.75 hierarchy; it was introduced in a SCOPe 2.x release after the 2012 TALE-DNA complexes were deposited. Cite the family with its release (for example SCOPe 2.07 or 2.08), since sunids, sids, and even fold numbering for recent additions are release-dependent, and d4cj9a_ in particular will only be present in releases that postdate its deposition.
